summary: AE + SE walked SierraData through Redwood Console and API features for org-level and project-level API keys, rate limiting, and quota controls. Key themes: per-org billing vs per-project quotas, burst allowances, enforcement points (edge vs runtime), and audit logging for multi-tenant setups. Agreed to a 2-week POC with seeded project keys.
topics: Org vs Project keys (auth model and scoping)
Rate limiting: per-project, per-route, and per-org quotas
Burst allowance and token bucket behaviour
Monitoring: per-key metrics in Console and Optimize suggestions
Security: key rotation, RBAC, audit logs, KMS integration
transcript: [00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, I'm Maya, AE at Redwood.
[00:10] Aisha Patel: Hi, Aisha here, CTO at SierraData. We're interested in how you handle multi-tenant rate limiting — we have multiple internal products sharing the same account.
[00:23] Diego Ortiz: Great — I'll run the console demo after we cover the high level. Quick question on scope: do you want strict per-tenant isolation or soft quotas with overage alerts?
[00:35] Tom Reilly: We need strict isolation for customer-facing workloads, dev teams can be softer. Ideally per-project keys map to teams and customer tenants.

[00:48] Maya Chen: Perfect. Today's walkthrough will show org keys, project keys, console policies, and the API side for enforcement. We'll also show Optimize suggestions for batching and cost controls.
[01:12] Lena Park: From security side we also care about key rotation and audit logs — and whether those logs show per-request metadata like project id and route.

[01:26] Diego Ortiz: Yes, audit logs include request id, key id, project id, route and token counts. We also surface it in the Console as a per-key activity timeline, and you can stream it to your SIEM.
[02:05] Maya Chen: Ok pulling up the Redwood Console — apologies if the UI looks slightly different, we have a recent update. On the left you see Organizations, Projects, and Keys.

[02:22] [screen share noises] Diego Ortiz: Here is the org view — top-level billing and global quotas. Under it we have Projects; each project has its own keys and quota. Note you can pin a budget per project or let it inherit the org cap.
[03:05] Jamal White: When you say "quota" is that token budget or request count? We bill and quota in tokens at SierraData.
[03:15] Diego Ortiz: Good call — our quotas are token-based by default, you can also configure request-count ceilings. For the POC we'll mirror your token-based accounting.

[03:38] Maya Chen: Now switching to Rate limits tab — you can create rules: scope (project|org), window (per-second/per-minute), limit (tokens or requests), and burst allowance. We'll create a demo rule for a project.

[04:05] [typing noises] Diego Ortiz: I'm adding a per-project rule: Project 'search-api' — 2000 tokens/sec with a burst of 4000 tokens and a cooldown window of 60s. Note: burst uses a token-bucket implementation so it smooths traffic.
[04:35] Tom Reilly: Is burst shared across sibling projects or per-key?
[04:42] Diego Ortiz: Per-key per-project. You can also choose to enable a global org buffer — e.g., small burst reserve that any project can consume if org budget allows.
[05:10] Maya Chen: Many customers use per-project strict limits for production services and looser org-level thresholds for internal tooling.
[05:24] Aisha Patel: When a key hits a limit, what's the default behavior — 429 or queued/backpressure?

[05:33] Diego Ortiz: By default we return a 429 with a Retry-After header. There's an optional queued policy available for Dedicated deployments that can hold requests for a short window (configurable) — not recommended for most low-latency APIs.
[06:00] Lena Park: For PCI/PHI workloads we can't expose request contents to Redwood; can we still get per-key auditing metadata?

[06:12] Maya Chen: Yes — metadata like key id, project id, model id, token counts, timestamp, and routing decision are logged. Request payload is not persisted unless you opt in under a retention contract; we do offer on-prem deployments for air-gapped setups.
[06:45] [brief crosstalk] Jamal White: You mentioned KMS earlier?
[06:50] Diego Ortiz: Correct — Redwood integrates with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) for key wrapping; on Private installs we support HSM. Key rotation can be automated via API.

[07:20] Maya Chen: I'll demo API usage next. Example: use org-key to create project-key via /v1/orgs/{org}/projects endpoint, then issue scoped key for a project with limited permissions (read-only or inference-only).

[07:50] [typing] Diego Ortiz: Live curl sample — curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/projects -H 'Authorization: Bearer ORG_KEY' -d '{"name":"search-api"}' — response includes project_id and project_key_secret. Note we never show full secret in UI; it's only displayed on creation.
[08:25] Tom Reilly: We want enforceable RBAC so only Platform team can create keys. Can that be enforced in Console?

[08:33] Diego Ortiz: Yes, RBAC is part of the Console. You can create roles (admin, dev, billing) and attach them at org or project scope. We support SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning users and groups.
[09:02] Aisha Patel: How do you meter usage for billing? We need per-tenant breakdowns for showback and chargeback.
[09:12] Maya Chen: Billing is org-level by default, but you can export per-project cost breakdown. The Console has cost allocation reports and CSV export; you can set per-project budget alerts too.

[09:45] Diego Ortiz: Also Optimize will suggest batching and quantization changes per project to meet cost targets while keeping quality. You can schedule a nightly job to run evals on your prompt set.
[10:20] Jamal White: Can Optimize auto-enforce configuration changes or only recommend?

[10:27] Priya Rao: Right now Optimize provides recommendations and suggested profiles. You can optionally approve automated rollouts for low-risk changes (e.g., apply a quantized variant for non-sensitive workloads).
[11:00] [longer jump — mid call, discussing enforcement edge cases]
[28:12] Tom Reilly: If we do a sudden spike from a customer, will the per-project limit cause cascading failures? We need circuit breakers upstream.

[28:23] Diego Ortiz: Good point. We recommend client-side retry/backoff plus server-side 429 handling. For dedicated customers you can enable graceful fallback to a cheaper model variant that you configure in routing policies.
[29:05] Aisha Patel: Is there support for per-route limits? e.g., embeddings vs chat endpoints having separate budgets.

[29:12] Diego Ortiz: Yes, rule scoping allows you to limit by route or model tag — e.g., /v1/embed -> 5000 tokens/min, /v1/chat -> 2000 tokens/min. We also let you define priorities so embeddings can be preempted in emergencies.
[38:40] Lena Park: Regarding logs, are they available in real time for security alerts? We need 30s-ish latency to push to our SIEM.
[38:48] Maya Chen: You can stream events to a webhook, Kinesis, or Pub/Sub. Delivery is typically sub-30s for streaming events; batched export is hourly/daily depending on retention.
[40:02] Tom Reilly: Do you have examples of rate limit policies for multi-tenant SaaS?

[40:10] Diego Ortiz: Yes — we have a template library in the Console. Example: 'Per-tenant production: 5k tokens/sec, burst 10k, org buffer 50k tokens/day' or 'Internal dev: 200 tokens/sec with no org buffer'. We'll share the templates.

[45:15] Maya Chen: Quick demo of a breach event — I'm triggering synthetic traffic to push a project over its limit. You can see the Console alert, the request spikes, and 429s returned. Also shows automatic email+Slack webhook that we wired for alerts.
[46:02] Jamal White: Nice. Can the alert include the offending key and sample rate?
[46:08] Diego Ortiz: Yes — alerts show key id, project id, current rate, threshold, and a link to the request trace. The trace links into the per-request timeline if you have tracing enabled.
[49:30] Aisha Patel: For the POC we want two seeded project keys: one for search-api and one for ingestion. We'll run a traffic replay and expect you to capture per-key metrics.
[49:42] Maya Chen: We'll provision that after the call. Diego will run a short benchmark and share the script. We'll also include the rate-limit config and the Optimize suggestions.
[52:05] Tom Reilly: What's the rollback plan if the POC causes noisy neighbor issues?

[52:13] Diego Ortiz: We'll set strict per-project limits in the POC and enable org buffer only for a small percentage. If noisy neighbor appears, we can quickly adjust project caps and use routing fallback to cheaper model to protect latency-sensitive routes.
[54:00] Lena Park: One last security Q: retention and deletion — if a tenant requests deletion, can you purge their infer logs?

[54:10] Maya Chen: Yes, redaction and per-tenant purge is supported for enterprise and Private deployments. There's a documented process and we can run it on demand; for hosted customers we maintain an audit trail of purge operations.
[55:20] Maya Chen: Recap — we'll send the rate-limit templates, security whitepaper, provision test org and project keys, and schedule POC kickoff. Any other asks?
[55:35] Aisha Patel: Please include a sample CSV of per-project billing exports so finance can verify allocation.
[55:45] Maya Chen: Will do. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and confirm kickoff time.
[56:05] [meeting ends]
